title: How AI systems work
desc: Follow the input → model → output pipeline with hands-on examples
content_html:
What We're Doing

Every AI system, no matter how clever it looks, is built from three parts: an input, a process in the middle, and an output. AI never works on its own — a person decides what goes in, what happens in the middle, and what comes out. In this lesson we learn to "see" those three parts inside the everyday AI tools around us, so AI stops feeling like magic and starts feeling like something we could design ourselves.

You'll Need

  • A whiteboard or large sheet of paper
  • Sticky notes or index cards
  • A short list of everyday AI tools to discuss (photo filter, voice assistant, video recommendations, map directions, spam filter)

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Draw the pipeline big on the board: INPUT → AI SYSTEM → OUTPUT.
  2. Work one example together out loud. A homework reminder app: Input = your homework dates; Process = the app checks today against the calendar; Output = a reminder pops up.
  3. Split into small groups. Each group picks three AI tools and, on sticky notes, labels the input, the process, and the output for each one.
  4. Groups post their notes on the board and present one. The class checks: does every example really have all three parts?
  5. Add a fourth box — Feedback — and discuss how the output can loop back to become new input. When you tap "like", that choice becomes new data the recommendation system learns from.

Examples

AI toolInputProcessOutput
Photo filterYour selfieFinds your face, maps featuresEdited picture
Voice assistantYour spoken questionTurns sound to text, searchesA spoken answer
Video appWhat you watched beforeFinds similar videosYour "recommended" list

Facilitation Tips

  • Keep it concrete — push for real tools the learners actually use, not textbook examples.
  • Every time someone says "it just knows", ask "what was the input, and who gave it?" to break the magic.
  • Stress that a human designed each stage and chose the data — AI is a tool people build, not a mind of its own.

Discussion Questions

  • For your favourite app, where does the input data come from, and did you choose to give it?
  • Who decides what a "good" output looks like?
  • What happens to the output if the input is wrong or missing?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Map a video game you like as input → process → output.
  • Medium: Find an AI where the output becomes new input (a feedback loop) and draw the loop.
  • Hard: Sketch an AI you would build to solve a problem at your school, labelling all three stages and the exact data it would need to learn from.
